Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (ut​+uux​+uxx​+uxxxx​=0)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation ut​+uux​+uxx​+uxxxx​=0 combines destabilizing long-wave growth, stabilizing fourth-order diffusion, and nonlinear transport. Its potential form is Φt​=−Φxx​−Φxxxx​+(Φx​)2, with u=−2Φx​. It arises as a long-wave phase amplitude equation near loss of the Benjamin-Feir stability condition. On a domain of period P, the zero solution's Fourier modes grow at rate k2−k4, k=2πn/P.

Primary periodic bifurcation of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation

Words: 88
Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation OurBigBook.com
Fix zero mean and period P in the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. At P=2π the first Fourier mode becomes neutral and all higher modes are damped. For k=2π/P, expand u=asin(kx)+bsin(2kx)+⋯. The first equations are a˙=λ1​a+kab/2+⋯, b˙=λ2​b−ka2/2+⋯, with λj​=(jk)2−(jk)4. Slaving the second harmonic gives a˙=λ1​a+k2a3/(4λ2​)+⋯. Since λ2​=−12 at onset, this is a supercritical bifurcation. The small nonzero branch is stable in the sense of orbital stability against disturbances of the same fixed period, modulo translation; stability against disturbances of larger period does not follow from this local argument.

Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
Green's identities relate volume integrals involving gradients and Laplacians to boundary values and normal derivatives. They follow from the divergence theorem and include Green's first identity, Green second identity and Green's third identity.

Green's third identity represents a function inside a domain through its boundary values, normal derivatives, and a volume term involving its Laplacian.

For smooth functions u,v on a region V,
∫V​(uΔv+∇u⋅∇v)dV=∫∂V​u∂n∂v​dS.

Gradient pairing with a boundary-constant function and a harmonic function (∫V​∇f⋅∇gdV=0)

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Green's first identity OurBigBook.com
If f is constant on the boundary and g is a regular harmonic function throughout a volume, the divergence theorem applied to f∇g gives ∫V​∇f⋅∇g=∫∂V​f∂n​g. The constant boundary value factors out; a second application of the divergence theorem makes the remaining flux ∫V​Δg=0. This requires enough regularity to use Green's first identity over the entire volume.
Boundary flux from a singular harmonic potential (∫∣x∣<a​∇(r/a)⋅∇(1/r)dV=−4π)
Words: 74
Gradient pairing with a boundary-constant function and a harmonic function OurBigBook.com
Although 1/r is harmonic away from the origin in three dimensions, it is not a regular harmonic function on a ball containing the origin. Its gradient is −r/r2, so the displayed improper volume integral follows by canceling the r2 in the spherical volume element. On the annulus ε<r<a, Green's first identity gives outer boundary contribution −4π and inner contribution 4πε/a, recovering the same limit. Its global Laplacian contains a Dirac delta distribution, so the regular-harmonic gradient-pairing theorem is inapplicable.

Maximum principle

Words: 120 Articles: 2
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A maximum principle bounds a solution through its boundary or initial data, often forbidding nonconstant solutions from attaining an interior extremum. Weak and strong versions depend on the differential operator and hypotheses. The maximum principle for harmonic functions and its strong counterpart are examples.

Strong maximum principle for harmonic functions

Words: 46
Maximum principle OurBigBook.com
If a harmonic function on a connected domain attains an interior maximum or minimum, it is constant. The mean value property forces equality throughout every sufficiently small ball around an interior extremum, and connectedness propagates the equality.
This is the strong harmonic instance of the maximum principle.

Maximum principle for harmonic functions

Words: 35
Maximum principle OurBigBook.com
A continuous function harmonic on a bounded domain attains its maximum and minimum on the boundary. Apply the strictly subharmonic result to u+ϵ∣x∣2 and let ϵ↓0, then apply the same argument to −u.

Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The one-dimensional equation ut​+uux​=νuxx​ combines nonlinear transport with diffusion. Positive ν gives the viscous Burgers equation; setting ν=0 gives the Inviscid Burgers equation.

Burgers' equation OurBigBook.com
The viscous Burgers equation adds diffusion with viscosity ν>0 to nonlinear transport. Smooth initial data remain smooth, and the diffusion regularizes the shocks of the Inviscid Burgers equation.

The cubic-flux variant replaces the quadratic conservative flux of Burgers' equation by −q3/3. Its inviscid characteristic speed is −q2, while positive diffusivity regularizes shock waves. It is not linearized by the usual Cole-Hopf transformation.

For a front written in s=Z+cθ connecting 0 at s=−∞ to nonzero β at s=+∞, one integration gives ϵc2q′=q−cq3/3. The endpoint condition fixes c=3/β2. Setting w=q2 gives a logistic equation and the displayed profile, with the sign of q selected by β. The propagation speed in the θ coordinate is −β2/3, agreeing with the Rankine-Hugoniot condition for flux −q3/3.

A localized negative-flux Burgers N-wave has initial profile −Uθ on ∣θ∣<L and zero outside, for U,L>0. The Cole-Hopf solution for a Burgers N-wave expresses its viscous evolution in Gaussian interval masses. In the vanishing-viscosity limit, the interior slope becomes −U/(1+UZ) and its entropy-shock fronts move to ±L1+UZ​.

ψ=1−Iα​(θ,L,Z)+Iα​(θ,La,Za)a−1/2eU(L2−θ2/a)/(4α).

Viscous Burgers equation OurBigBook.com
For positive diffusivity, the Cole-Hopf transformation with f=2α∂θ​logψ converts the negative-flux equation into the heat equation. Step data give a ratio of two Gaussian-tail integrals J. At θ=−UZ/2, J=1 and f=U/2. Its vanishing-viscosity limit selects the shock or rarefaction wave in the Burgers Riemann problem with negative flux, depending on the sign of U.
Midpoint symmetry of a viscous Burgers step (f(z,−Uz−θ)=U−f(z,θ))
Words: 57
Viscous Burgers step solution with negative flux OurBigBook.com
The viscous Burgers step solution with negative flux is symmetric around θ=−Uz/2 after subtracting U/2. Its Gaussian-tail ratio equals one precisely at this midpoint, giving f=U/2 for either sign of U. For U>0 this point becomes the entropy-shock center in the vanishing viscosity approximation; for U<0 it is the center of a rarefaction wave. The same trajectory therefore does not by itself identify a shock.

For ordered states q1​<⋯<qN​, in the moving frame θ=sZ+ξ the first and last exponents in the finite-exponential Cole-Hopf solution have the same leading coefficient. Each interior state's coefficient is smaller by (qj​−q1​)(qN​−qj​)/(4ϵ)>0. Thus the large-Z moving-frame profile is the two-state shock between the extremes. At fixed θ, the endpoint of largest absolute value dominates; equal opposite extremes leave a stationary shock.

Semilinear partial differential equation

Words: 72 Articles: 1
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A semilinear partial differential equation is linear in its highest-order derivatives, with their coefficients depending only on the independent variables; lower-order terms may depend nonlinearly on the solution and its lower derivatives. A semilinear heat equation such as ut​=Δu+f(u) is an example. This differs from a quasilinear equation, whose highest-order derivative coefficients can depend on the solution or its lower derivatives.

Semilinear heat equation (ut​=Δu+f(u))

Semilinear partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A heat equation with a nonlinear reaction term depending on the value of its solution.

Obstacle problem

Words: 48
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
An obstacle constraint requires a solution to lie above a given function. In an optimal stopping problem, the value dominates the payoff, satisfies a generator equation where continuation is optimal, and a generator inequality where stopping is optimal. The complementary conditions can be expressed as a maximum equal to zero.

Parabolic comparison principle

Words: 134 Articles: 1
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A first-contact argument compares a smooth solution with a subsolution or supersolution. At a first spatial minimum of their difference, the Hessian is nonnegative; a strictly favorable time derivative then contradicts contact. For ut​=u2uxx​+u3, a positive decreasing constant-in-space barrier proves that positive periodic initial data stay positive for the lifetime of the smooth solution.

Invariant interval for a cubic reaction-diffusion equation (∣u∣≤max(∥u0​∥∞​,max(λ,0)​))

Words: 79
Parabolic comparison principle OurBigBook.com
For ut​=Δu+λu−u3 with zero Dirichlet boundary condition, choose K≥max(∥u0​∥∞​,max(λ,0)​). The constants K and −K are a supersolution and a subsolution. More explicitly, testing with (u−K)+​ gives 21​dtd​∥(u−K)+​∥22​≤λ∥(u−K)+​∥22​, since the reaction derivative is at most λ and the reaction at K is nonpositive. The Gronwall inequality and the corresponding argument for −u prove that [−K,K] is invariant. A local variation-of-constants formula in the supremum norm then has a lifespan depending only on K, which prevents finite-time loss of the classical solution.

Domain of dependence

Words: 81
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The domain of dependence of a solution value consists of the initial and boundary locations whose data can influence it. For ut​+aux​=0 on the whole line, u(x,t)=u(x−at,0), so its initial-data domain of dependence is the foot of the characteristic. For a finite-difference scheme, repeated stencil dependencies determine a numerical domain of dependence. The Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition requires the numerical domain to cover the physical one for convergence; it is necessary under its usual hyperbolic hypotheses, but not in general sufficient for stability.

Linear partial differential equation

Words: 28
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A linear partial differential equation is a partial differential equation in which the unknown function and its partial derivatives occur linearly, with coefficients independent of the unknown. Its homogeneous solutions obey the superposition principle.

Ill-posed problem

Words: 34
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
An ill-posed problem fails existence, uniqueness or continuous dependence in the specified function spaces. Backward heat equation evolution is unstable because its Fourier modes grow like et∣ξ∣2, making arbitrarily small high-frequency errors grow without a uniform bound.

Linear partial differential operator (P(D))

Words: 32
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A linear partial differential operator sends a function to a linear combination of its partial derivatives. If its coefficients are constant, the Fourier transform of a derivative turns it into multiplication by its polynomial symbol P(ξ).

Liouville equation (Δu=e2u)

Words: 19
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The elliptic Liouville equation Δu=e2u describes conformal metrics of constant negative Gaussian curvature under a common sign convention.

Radial function (f(x)=g(∣x∣))

Words: 25
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A radial function depends only on the distance from the origin: f(x)=g(∣x∣). Differential operators then reduce to radial formulas such as Δf=g′′+(n−1)g′/r.

Periodic domain

Words: 30
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A periodic domain identifies opposite faces of a fundamental cell, producing a flat torus. Periodic integration by parts has no boundary term, and zero-mean functions have no zero Fourier mode.

Energy estimate

Words: 675 Articles: 13
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
An energy estimate tests a differential equation against the solution or one of its derivatives to control a norm by initial data and forcing. Coercive terms represent dissipation, while Young inequality and the Gronwall inequality control lower-order terms.

Bootstrap argument

Words: 54

Symmetry reduction of a partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
